title: What if you could SEE Wi-Fi? 📶
description:
Wi-Fi is light too, with waves about 12 cm long instead of 400-700 nanometres. To see it as sharply as you see now, your eyes would need to be about a kilometre wide, which is why radio telescopes like FAST are huge.

Sources: Wikipedia (2.4 GHz radio use, visible spectrum, FAST); NCBI/PMC on bees, flowers and UV; OpenStax Astronomy on why radio telescopes must be so large.

meta.topic: what if you could see Wi-Fi: visible light vs 12 cm Wi-Fi waves, why your eyes would need to be ~1 km wide (diffraction), FAST dish
meta.idea_source: unique + viral-shaped: everyday object (Wi-Fi) made into a physics what-if; owner's 'what is a spectrum' example

humour.trend: timeless (no current trend fit cleanly): the hunt for the one full-bars Wi-Fi spot, smirk + caption card

claims.claim: Wi-Fi/radio waves are electromagnetic radiation, the same family as visible light
human eyes detect roughly 400-700 nm (often quoted 380-750 nm)
bees see ultraviolet; many flowers have UV nectar guides
2.4 GHz Wi-Fi has a wavelength of ~12.5 cm
router glowing / walls see-through if eyes caught 12 cm waves
diffraction limit: same sharpness at 12.5 cm as a 5 mm pupil at 550 nm needs an aperture of ~1.1 km (theta ~ 1.22 lambda/D)
FAST, China's radio telescope, has a 500 m dish; radio telescopes are large because of long wavelengths

speaker: ved

scenes.say: What if you could *see* Wi-Fi? It's light too.
Your eyes catch just *400 to 700 nanometres*.
